title: Hand examination: Dupuytren's disease or rheumatoid hand

guidelineVersions: GIRFT hand surgery pathway: Dupuytren's disease (July 2026)

brief.scenario: Mr Frank Ingram, 66, a retired joiner, is right-handed. Over three years the ring and little fingers of his right hand have curled into his palm. They catch when he puts his hand in his pocket.
brief.task: Examine his hands. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to present your findings and answer questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Look, feel, move, function, then nerves and circulation; both hands, palm and back.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Calling every bent finger rheumatoid, or offering an injection that is no longer available in the UK.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Could you roll your sleeves up and rest both hands on this pillow, palms down?"

grid.label: Preparation and exposure
grid.fail: Examines one hand with the sleeves down and doesn't ask about pain.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, gains consent, cleans hands, asks about pain, and exposes both forearms with the hands on a pillow.
grid.high: Asks about hand dominance, work and daily tasks first, and compares both hands at every step.

grid.label: Look: dorsum, palm and elbows
grid.fail: Looks only at the palm of the affected hand.
grid.pass: Inspects dorsum and palm: nodules, cords, skin pits, finger posture, joint swelling, scars and wasting; looks at the elbows.
grid.high: Names the rays involved, looks for Garrod's knuckle pads, and asks about lumps in the soles.

grid.label: Feel: cords, nodules and joints
grid.fail: Doesn't touch the palm or the joints.
grid.pass: Palpates the nodules and cords, notes skin tethering, and feels the wrist, MCP and PIP joints for swelling or tenderness.
grid.high: Traces each cord from the palm into the finger, and states there is no synovitis, which separates a cord from inflammatory joint disease.

grid.label: Move: fixed flexion and tabletop test
grid.fail: Records 'bent fingers' without separating active from passive movement.
grid.borderline: Performs the tabletop test but doesn't say which joints are fixed.
grid.pass: Tests active and passive extension, shows the flexion is fixed, and performs the tabletop test.
grid.high: Measures the fixed flexion at each MCP and PIP joint separately, finger by finger, with a goniometer.

grid.label: Function, sensation and circulation
grid.pass: Tests grip, pinch and a task such as a button; checks sensation on both sides of each affected finger, and capillary refill.
grid.high: Records digital nerve sensation before any procedure, because a cord can displace the digital nerve.

grid.label: Dupuytren's or rheumatoid hand
grid.fail: Calls it rheumatoid arthritis because the fingers are bent.
grid.pass: Contrasts palmar cords with normal joints against rheumatoid synovitis, ulnar deviation, swan-neck or boutonnière deformity and nodules.
grid.high: Adds that suspected persistent synovitis of the small hand joints needs urgent rheumatology referral, even with a negative rheumatoid factor.

grid.label: Presentation at the signal
grid.fail: Lists what was done, with no conclusion.
grid.pass: Presents the digits and joints involved, function, and a diagnosis.
grid.high: Leads with the diagnosis and severity: right Dupuytren's disease, ring and little fingers, fixed MCP and PIP flexion, positive tabletop test, no synovitis.

grid.label: When and how to treat
grid.fail: Offers collagenase injection, or surgery for a finger that straightens fully.
grid.pass: Refers to hand surgery once the hand can't lie flat; options are needle fasciotomy or fasciectomy, with dermofasciectomy mainly for recurrence.
grid.high: Quotes the pathway threshold: 30° or more at the MCP joint or 20° at the PIP joint; knows collagenase is unavailable in the UK.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Takes the right hand, sleeve still down.] Which one is it? Right.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Looks at the palm.] The fingers are bent. [Doesn't feel the palm or joints.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Can you straighten them? No. [Doesn't test passive movement or the tabletop test.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: His fingers are bent, so I think this is rheumatoid arthritis.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A collagenase injection into the cord in clinic.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Osei, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? I'd like to examine both hands. Any pain? Could you roll your sleeves up and rest your hands on the pillow? [Consent; cleans hands.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Inspects dorsum, then palm, then elbows.] There are cords to the right ring and little fingers, with pitting in the palm. No joint swelling, no wasting, no scars.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Tell me if anything's tender. [Palpates nodules and cords; feels wrist, MCP and PIP joints.] The skin is tethered over the cord; the joints aren't swollen.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Straighten your fingers for me. [Then gently tries passively.] They won't go straight either way, so the flexion is fixed. Can you put your hand flat on the table? [Tabletop test positive.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Squeeze my fingers; pinch this; undo this button. [Light touch on both sides of each affected finger; capillary refill.] Thank you. [Cleans hands.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mr Ingram has palmar cords to the right ring and little fingers with fixed flexion at the MCP and PIP joints, and a positive tabletop test. Sensation and circulation are normal. This is Dupuytren's disease.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How do you know it isn't rheumatoid arthritis?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: There are cords in the palm and the joints are normal. In rheumatoid arthritis I'd expect synovitis, ulnar deviation, swan-neck or boutonnière deformities, and rheumatoid nodules.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: His hand won't lie flat, so I'd refer him to the hand surgeons to discuss needle fasciotomy or fasciectomy. Dermofasciectomy is mainly used for recurrence.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Osei, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? Which is your writing hand, and what can't you do because of your fingers? I'll compare both hands throughout. [Cleans hands.]

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Inspects.] Right ring and little finger rays involved. Garrod's knuckle pads over two knuckles. Have you noticed any lumps in the soles of your feet?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Traces each cord from the palm into the finger.] The cord runs into the little finger. The wrist and finger joints aren't warm, swollen or tender: no synovitis.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Goniometer, joint by joint.] Ring finger: MCP about 40 degrees, PIP 10. Little finger: MCP 20, PIP 35. All fixed.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Checks sensation on both sides of each affected finger.] I'd record digital nerve sensation before any procedure, because the cord can push the nerve out of its usual position. [Cleans hands.]

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Mr Ingram has right Dupuytren's disease of the ring and little fingers, with fixed MCP and PIP flexion and a positive tabletop test. There's no synovitis, and sensation is intact. His left palm has an early nodule only.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How do you know it isn't rheumatoid arthritis?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The deformity comes from palmar cords, not the joints. If I found persistent synovitis in the small joints of the hand, I'd refer urgently to rheumatology, even with a negative rheumatoid factor.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He meets the pathway's surgical threshold: 30 degrees or more at the MCP joint or 20 at the PIP. Needle fasciotomy or fasciectomy are the options. Collagenase is no longer available in the UK.

failures.move: Not separating active from passive extension.
failures.consequence: A fixed contracture can't be told apart from a tendon or nerve problem, and the severity isn't recorded.
Wrong referral; and in a genuine rheumatoid hand, synovitis may not be referred urgently.
A nerve deficit found after surgery can't be shown to have been present before it.
Xiapex is no longer available in the UK, and NICE has withdrawn TA459.

recovery.line: Before I finish, could you put your hand flat on the table for me?

recovery.when: The examiner asks about an injection
recovery.line: Collagenase isn't available in the UK now, so the options are needle fasciotomy or surgery.

knowledge.fact: Ring finger is most often affected, then little and middle. Surgical threshold: 30° or more at the MCPJ or 20° at the PIPJ, a thumb contracture impairing function, or rapid progression.
No surgery if the finger straightens fully. Dermofasciectomy is usually for recurrence, or extensive disease in a younger person. Disease can recur.
Needle fasciotomy: NICE judges the evidence adequate with normal consent and audit.
Collagenase (Xiapex) is no longer available in the UK; TA459 is withdrawn.
Rheumatoid hand with imminent or actual tendon rupture: specialist surgical opinion before damage is irreversible.

recall.think: Is this Dupuytren's or inflammatory arthritis, and does it need surgery?
recall.say: "Palmar cords, fixed flexion and no synovitis: Dupuytren's disease."
do: Look at palm, dorsum and elbows
Feel cords and joints; tabletop test
recall.trap: Offering collagenase: it is no longer available in the UK.
recall.finish: Hand surgery referral: needle fasciotomy, fasciectomy or dermofasciectomy.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Introduce yourself, confirm identity, obtain consent and clean hands at every station; 6-minute signal in examination stations

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Hand examination sequence (look, feel, move, function); rheumatoid hand deformities; digital nerve displaced by Dupuytren's cords

sources.name: GIRFT Best Practice Library (NHS England): Hand surgery pathway: Dupuytren's disease
sources.supports: Findings: skin thickening or pitting in the palm, firm fixed nodules, fibrous cords, flexion deformity of MCP and IP joints, loss of hand function, unable to lay palm and fingers flat on a table top; ring finger most commonly affected, followed by little and middle fingers; threshold for surgery: flexion contracture of 30° or more at the MCPJ or 20° at the PIPJ, thumb contracture impairing function, failed non-operative management, rapidly progressive disease; percutaneous fasciotomy in outpatients or listing for day case surgery; consider injecting intolerably painful nodules with cortisone; BSSH patient information

sources.name: British Society for Surgery of the Hand: Dupuytren's disease (patient information)
sources.supports: Nodules and cords in the palm, skin pits, Garrod's knuckle pads, lumps in the soles; often begins in line with the ring finger; surgery not needed if the finger straightens fully; discuss with a surgeon once the hand can't be put flat on a table; fasciotomy, segmental or regional fasciectomy, dermofasciectomy (usually for recurrent disease, or extensive disease in a younger person); disease may recur in operated or new areas

sources.name: NICE TA459: Collagenase clostridium histolyticum for treating Dupuytren's contracture
sources.supports: NICE has withdrawn the guidance because collagenase clostridium histolyticum (Xiapex) is no longer available in the UK

sources.name: NICE HTG21 (formerly IPG43): Needle fasciotomy for Dupuytren's contracture
sources.supports: Evidence on safety and efficacy appears adequate to support needle fasciotomy, provided normal arrangements are in place for consent, audit and clinical governance (1.1)

sources.name: NICE NG100: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management
sources.supports: Refer suspected persistent synovitis for specialist opinion, urgently (even with normal acute-phase response or negative anti-CCP or rheumatoid factor) if small joints of the hands or feet or more than one joint are affected, or after a delay of 3 months or more (1.1.1); offer referral for a specialist surgical opinion before damage becomes irreversible for imminent or actual tendon rupture, nerve compression or stress fracture (1.10.2); suspected cervical myelopathy: urgent MRI and specialist surgical opinion (1.10.5)

partner.opening: Please examine this patient's hands. I'll stop you at 6 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Mr Frank Ingram, 66, a retired joiner, right-handed. Your right ring and little fingers have slowly curled into your palm over three years. They catch when you put your hand in your pocket or wash your face. No pain, no joint swelling, no morning stiffness. Your father had the same thing. If asked, you have a small lump in the sole of your right foot. Keep your right ring and little fingers bent throughout.

reveals.finding: Right: palmar nodule and cord to the ring finger, a second cord to the little finger, skin pitting at the distal palmar crease. Knuckle pads over the right index and middle PIP joints. No joint swelling, ulnar deviation, wasting, scars, psoriasis or elbow nodules. Left: small palmar nodule in line with the ring finger.
Firm, non-tender cords; skin tethered over them. Wrist, MCP and PIP joints not warm, swollen or tender.
Neither actively nor passively correctable. Ring finger: MCP about 40° fixed flexion, PIP about 10°. Little finger: MCP about 20°, PIP about 35°. Left hand extends fully.
Right: cannot lay the palm and fingers flat. Left: lies flat.
Grip and pinch good; manages a button slowly. Light touch normal on both sides of each finger. Capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Say: "Please stop there and present your findings."

push.question: Which features separate this from a rheumatoid hand?
push.expect: Palmar cords and nodules with normal joints; no synovitis, ulnar deviation, swan-neck or boutonnière deformity, or rheumatoid nodules.

push.question: When is surgery indicated?
push.expect: Hand can't lie flat; GIRFT threshold 30° or more at the MCP joint or 20° at the PIP joint; thumb contracture affecting function; rapid progression.

push.question: What are the treatment options?
push.expect: Needle fasciotomy, limited or regional fasciectomy, dermofasciectomy (mainly for recurrence). Collagenase is no longer available in the UK.

curveballs.prompt: He says a friend had an injection instead of an operation.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Collagenase (Xiapex) is no longer available in the UK and NICE has withdrawn TA459; needle fasciotomy is the less invasive option.

curveballs.prompt: A different patient has a painful palmar nodule, but every finger straightens fully.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No surgery if the fingers straighten fully; the pathway suggests a steroid injection for intolerably painful nodules, and review if it progresses.

curveballs.prompt: A woman with known rheumatoid arthritis suddenly can't extend her ring and little fingers.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Likely extensor tendon rupture: refer for a specialist surgical opinion before the damage becomes irreversible.

curveballs.prompt: A rheumatoid patient describes tingling hands, unsteadiness and has extensor plantars.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Suspected cervical myelopathy: urgent MRI and specialist surgical opinion.
